summary: For ages 5-6: children observe that sunlight warms Earth's surfaces — ground, water, rocks and objects in the sun feel warmer than the same things in the shade. Learning is strictly relative and sensory (warmer/cooler by touch or a simple relative thermometer or colour strip), with no degrees, no mechanism and no light-vs-heat theory. The core win is the observed cause: sun reaching a surface warms it; shade is cooler because it blocks the sun's warmth, not because it sends out cold. Firsthand outdoor observation is the heart of this objective; screen activities rehearse the cause and prediction and should accompany, not replace, real touching and leaving-and-revisiting.
misconceptions: 'Shade makes things cold' — rather than shade simply blocking the sun so the area doesn't get warmed; the cool is the absence of warming, not a cold source.
Thinking everything in the sun is equally warm — dark/heavier things warm more (a real effect, kept as enrichment, not the core claim).
Conflating the sun's LIGHT and its WARMTH, or believing only light (not warmth) reaches us — here the focus is the warming effect.
'Things stay warm by themselves' — not noticing that without the sun (shade, night) surfaces cool down again.
Believing sunlight can't warm water or see-through things — water and clear objects in the sun warm too.

activities.title: Touch the sun, touch the shade (firsthand outdoor observation)
steps: Go outside and touch the same kind of surface in two spots — e.g. sunny tarmac vs shaded tarmac, sunny grass vs shaded grass, or a sunny windowsill vs a shaded one — and say which feels warmer.
Keep the comparison fair: same object or surface, two spots (one sunny, one shaded), checked at the same time, so the sun is the only difference.
After touching, confirm warmer/cooler with a simple relative thermometer or colour-changing temperature strip if available — staying relative, never reading out degrees.
Say in plain words what was felt: 'the Sun warms it up; in the shade the sun can't reach it, so it stays cooler.'
activities.insight: Sunlight reaching a surface warms it; a shaded spot is cooler because the sun's warmth is blocked, not because shade makes cold.

activities.title: Leave and revisit: two cups in sun and shade
steps: Put two identical cups of water filled from the same jug (or two matching rocks), so they start out equally warm, outside — one in full sun, one in shade.
Before leaving them, predict which will be warmer later and say why.
Return after a while and compare with hands or a relative thermometer; talk about what changed and whether the prediction held.
Optionally revisit the same sunny spot after a short time and again a little later to notice warmth can build up the longer it sits in the sun.
activities.insight: The sun is the source of the extra warmth that builds up over time; the shaded item stays cooler than the sunny one because the sun's warmth does not reach it.

activities.title: Sunny-day sandbox (on-screen cause-and-prediction rehearsal)
steps: Drag an object (a rock, a cup of water, a metal slide, sand) between a sunny patch and a shaded patch on screen.
Watch a simple warm/cool meter and a colour or glow cue respond live as the object moves into the sun or into the shade.

Slide a cloud or umbrella over the sun and watch the modelled scene cool — noting this is a simplified model that cools quickly, whereas a real warm surface would cool gradually once the sun is blocked.
Before moving an object, predict out loud whether it will get warmer or cooler, then move it and check.
activities.insight: You control the warmth by controlling whether the sun reaches the object — sun on it = warmer, blocked = cooler — and you can predict the result before acting.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal sunny scene (reference observation)
steps: In a single sunny outdoor scene, tap the rock, the puddle, the slide or the shaded bench.
Hear which is 'warm — the sun is shining on it' or 'cool — it's in the shade' with picture-and-audio.
Tap a flap on the sun that says 'I warm things up.'
activities.insight: Objects the sun shines on are warmer; objects in shade are cooler because the sun is blocked.

activities.title: Which feels warmer? (sorting check)
steps: Sort pictured objects into 'in the sun = warmer' vs 'in the shade = cooler' using picture-and-audio.
Answer a 'which feels warmer?' picture choice using relative language only.
Try tricky cases: a clear cup of water or a see-through object in the sun also warms up.
activities.insight: Children can apply the sun-warms / shade-cooler rule to new objects, including water and clear things.

checkQuestion: On a sunny day the bench in the sun feels warm but the bench under the tree feels cooler. A friend says 'the shade makes it cold.' Do you agree — what is really making the shady bench cooler?
checkAnswer: The shady bench is cooler because the tree blocks the sun's light and warmth from reaching it — the sun isn't warming it up. The shade doesn't make cold or send out coldness; 'cooler' just means less of the sun's warming got there.
